content: The introduction of medical abortion has significantly enhanced access to safe abortion procedures. Medical abortion typically involves the administration of mifepristone followed by misoprostol or, alternatively, a misoprostol-only regimen. These medications are often given under the supervision of healthcare professionals, a process referred to as provider-administered medical abortion. In contrast, self-administered medical abortion allows women to take the medications themselves without direct supervision from a healthcare provider during at least one stage of the protocol. Self-administration offers women greater autonomy over the abortion process. In regions with limited healthcare resources, this approach may alleviate the strain on healthcare systems. However, the safety and efficacy of self-administered medical abortion remain uncertain. It is crucial to determine whether women can safely and effectively terminate pregnancies when provided with accurate information, high-quality medications, and access to medical care in case of complications. The objective of this review was to compare the effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of self-administered versus provider-administered medical abortion in any setting. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, POPLINE, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO ICTRP, and Google Scholar, covering studies up to July 10, 2019. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective cohort studies with concurrent comparison groups. These studies compared self-administered and provider-administered medical abortion methods. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers, and meta-analyses were conducted where appropriate using Review Manager 5. The primary outcome was the success of the abortion, defined as complete uterine evacuation without the need for surgical intervention. Secondary outcomes included ongoing pregnancy, defined as the presence of an intact gestational sac. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Chi-squared tests and I-squared statistics, with a significance threshold of P < 0.10. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach, following standard Cochrane methodological procedures. The review identified 18 studies involving 11,043 women undergoing early medical abortion (≤9 weeks gestation) across 10 countries. Sixteen studies were conducted in lowto middle-income settings, while two were in high-resource settings. Among the studies, one non-randomized study (NRS) received analgesics from a pharmaceutical company, five NRSs and one RCT did not disclose funding sources, nine NRSs were funded by anonymous donors, and five NRSs and one RCT received funding from government agencies, private foundations, or non-profit organizations. The intervention primarily involved women taking mifepristone under healthcare provider supervision, followed by self-administration of misoprostol (e.g., at home). The evidence showed no significant difference in the success rates of abortion between self-administered and provider-administered groups. For two RCTs, the risk ratio (RR) was 0.99 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.97 to 1.01) with moderate certainty of evidence, involving 919 participants. For 16 NRSs, the RR was also 0.99 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.01) with very low certainty of evidence, involving 10,124 participants. Regarding ongoing pregnancy, there appeared to be little or no difference between the two groups. For one RCT, the RR was 1.69 (95% CI 0.41 to 7.02) with low certainty of evidence, involving 735 participants. For 11 NRSs, the RR was 1.28 (95% CI 0.65 to 2.49) with very low certainty of evidence, involving 6,691 participants. The review found insufficient evidence to determine differences in complications requiring surgical intervention. No RCTs addressed this outcome, and evidence from three NRSs was of very low certainty, with an RR of 2.14 (95% CI 0.80 to 5.71) involving 2,452 participants. In conclusion, the review suggests that self-administering the second stage of early medical abortion procedures is as effective as provider-administered methods in terms of abortion success. There may be no difference in the outcome of ongoing pregnancy, although the evidence for this is uncertain. The evidence for complications requiring surgical intervention is of very low certainty. The findings are limited by the lack of high-quality studies and potential biases in the available data. The review highlights the need for further research to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of self-administered medical abortion without healthcare provider supervision throughout the entire protocol, including the administration of mifepristone or a misoprostol-only regimen. Future studies should also explore self-administration at later gestational ages (beyond nine weeks). Additionally, research is needed to identify the best ways to inform and support women who choose self-administration, including guidance on when to seek clinical care.
